claims.text: At stage-2 Order.Status has a private setter; the constructor sets "new", MarkPaid() "paid", Cancel() "cancelled", Ship() "shipped"; each checks the starting status, else throws OrderStatusException, and none reads or changes a Product. No code sets an order to "failed".

At stage-2 Notification is declared in the same Entities.cs as Order, with a public `required string Status`, Attempts, NextAttemptAt, an int OrderId (each notification belongs to one order) and an Order navigation; the comment above it names pending, sent and failed.

Notification.Status is set outside the class: pending when the email is queued (QueuedNotifier.Send), sent or failed in NotificationSender; DonHangDbContext adds check constraint notifications_status_check allowing only pending, sent, failed.

At stage-2 one DonHangDbContext declares DbSets for Customer, Product, Order, OrderItem, Payment and Notification, in one PostgreSQL database. Payment (Entities.cs:107-114) is used by no code outside Entities.cs and DonHangDbContext.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang @ stage-2: DonHang.Infrastructure/DonHangDbContext.cs:7-14; DonHang.Domain/Entities.cs:107-114; git grep -n Payment stage-2 -- '*.cs'

claims.text: NotificationSender.SendOneAsync takes the customer as notification.Order!.Customer! and uses its Email and FullName to send the email, then sets Status "sent" and SentAt; on an exception it calls RecordFailure.

At stage-2 nothing in the build or the tests forbids code from reading another context's classes: the only architecture test, DependencyRuleTests, checks that DonHang.Domain references no outer assembly.

At stage-2 Product has only Id, Name and PriceVnd: no status, no methods. Its one check, price above zero, is in db/schema.sql (CHECK (price_vnd > 0)) and in UpdateProductPriceRequest ([Range(1, int.MaxValue)]), not in the class.
ProductsController.List starts from db.Products (DonHangDbContext) and applies an optional Where, OrderBy, Skip, Take and Select; its comment says it has no rule to apply, only a query to shape.
Entities.cs is organised one class per table: its header comment says "One class per table in db/schema.sql".
Order refers to its customer by CustomerId; Customer.IdentitySubject holds Keycloak's id for the person.

Order's private parameterless constructor sets Status = "" and exists for EF Core only (comment above it); EF Core calls it when materializing an order from a query, then sets the mapped properties, including Status, from the row.

claims.text: git grep: -n prints line numbers, -w matches the pattern only at word boundaries, a tree-ish argument such as a tag searches the files as they are there, and paths after -- limit the search.
A bounded context is drawn where a model's words and rules stop, not by projects, folders or databases; one project and one database can hold several.
claims.source_hint: Domain-Driven Design (Evans), Part IV, Bounded Context

claims.text: Where to draw the lines is a design choice; one reasonable reading of stage-2 is three contexts with Keycloak outside; notifications could be read as part of ordering since each belongs to one order; the catalogue reading is weaker (no rules in its class rather than different ones).
When the lines are still moving, splitting projects early fixes in place a boundary the team may soon redraw.
An aggregate is one unit of change that keeps its invariants; a bounded context is where a language applies and can hold several aggregates, as ordering holds Order and Customer.
claims.source_hint: Domain-Driven Design (Evans), Aggregates and Bounded Context; design.l3.reference-other-aggregates-by-id
